items.title: Myanmar Committed Genocide Against the Rohingya, Top Global Court Finds
items.summary: In a decision with potentially broad implications, the International Court of Justice found a state culpable of genocide for the first time.
items.full_text:
Title: Myanmar Committed Genocide Against the Rohingya, Top Global Court Finds - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/world/europe/myanmar-genocide-icj-decision-.html

Published Time: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 18:00:21 GMT

Markdown Content:
The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, a landmark decision years in the making that makes the Southeast Asian nation the first state to be held to account for violating the [1948 Genocide Convention](https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/convention-prevention-and-punishment-crime-genocide).

The ruling covers Myanmar’s deadly military campaign against the Rohingya minority, which killed at least 10,000 people in a few weeks in 2017 and forced three quarters of a million people to flee during that same period. More deaths and expulsions followed.

“The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in Northern Rakhine state,” Judge Yuji Iwasawa, the president of the ICJ, said while reading the court’s decision on Thursday. The decision was made by 9 votes to 6.

The decision could have sweeping implications, including for another genocide case before the I.C.J., the United Nations’ highest judicial body: the accusation of genocide by Israel against the people of the Gaza Strip.

Image

Rohingya refugees who fled violence in Myanmar on foot continue their journey to a refugee camp in Bangladesh, in 2017.Credit...Tomas Munita for The New York Times

A spokeswoman for the government of Myanmar, in the capital Naypyidaw, did not answer a phone call seeking comment after the verdict was handed down. Myanmar authorities have previously disputed the charge.

Among [other findings,](https://www.icj-cij.org/sites/default/files/case-related/178/178-20261119-sum-01-00-en.pdf) the court determined that Myanmar had failed to prevent genocide. While it was not found to have incited private people to commit genocide, the court found that it also failed to punish genocide.

“This is a case a decade in the making,” said Juliette McIntyre, a Senior Lecturer in Law at Adelaide University in Australia. “From the point of view of the Rohingya people, who have been waiting, and waiting, and waiting for justice, this is very important.”

Gambia filed suit against Myanmar in 2019 in the court, which is based in The Hague. While the West African country is thousands of miles from Myanmar, international law gives countries the ability to act against genocide anywhere in the world — even if they are not affected.

In the Jamtoli camp of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, people thronged to a public viewing party to watch the hourslong decision, cheering and weeping as the decision was read. Some held signs that said “thank you, Gambia.”

Image

Rohingya refugees watch a live recording of the ICJ ruling in a refugee camp in Bangladesh,Credit...Lam Yik Fei for The New York Times

In The Hague, Dawda Jallow, the attorney general for Gambia, welcomed the decision to find Myanmar culpable of the “crime of crimes.” Speaking to journalists on the main staircase of the I.C.J.’s Peace Palace shortly after the ruling was read, he said, “we will stand with the Rohingya until justice is served.”

The violence at the core of the case took place in Myanmar’s far western Rakhine state, starting in 2016 and worsening in 2017. [U.N. officials](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/09/11/world/asia/myanmar-rohingya-ethnic-cleansing.html) and human rights groups have called it a coordinated, scorched-earth campaign to [remove the Rohingya](https://www.nytimes.com/2018/08/27/world/asia/myanmar-rohingya-genocide.html) — one that involved killing, wounding and raping, razing villages, and eventually forcing the expulsion of more than a million people to neighboring Bangladesh.

The Rohingya Muslims have a long history of [repression](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/10/24/world/asia/myanmar-rohingya-ethnic-cleansing.html) in Myanmar. After the nation’s independence from Britain in 1948, they were one of many ethnic groups in the country, which was then known as Burma. But over time, they faced [increasing](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/10/24/world/asia/myanmar-rohingya-ethnic-cleansing.html) attacks from members of the nation’s Buddhist majority.

A restrictive citizenship law in 1982 effectively rendered most Rohingya stateless. Various Myanmar governments, including a civilian authority led by the Nobel peace laureate Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, have refused to even acknowledge the Rohingya as a legitimate ethnic group, falsely referring to them instead as interlopers from neighboring Bangladesh.

Image

The remains of a destroyed mosque in the razed Rohingya village, Sabal Kone, Muangdaw Township, Myanmar in 2019.Credit...Adam Dean for The New York Times

Myanmar’s military called its campaign against the Rohingya “clearance operations.” Ms. Aung San Suu Kyi defended the military at the I.C.J., denying it committed genocide, before her government was deposed by the military and she was imprisoned in 2021. (After the coup, Myanmar descended into a civil war that is [still raging](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/27/world/asia/myanmar-light-aircraft-war-weapons.html).) About 1.2 million Rohingya now live in dire conditions in overcrowded camps in Bangladesh. Following the eruption of Myanmar’s [civil war](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/24/world/asia/myanmar-civil-war-rebels-airstrikes.html) in 2021, much of the Rohingya homeland is now controlled by a milita from the [Rakhine ethnic minority](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/12/28/world/asia/myanmar-rohingya-abuse.html), which has also been accused of persecuting Rohingya.

Thursday’s decision hinged on whether Myanmar acted with the specific intent to physically destroy the Rohingya, in whole or in part, as an ethnic or religious group.

The court found that Myanmar took measures to wipe out the Rohingya people, who did constitute a protected ethnic group by the court’s judgment.

The [case summary states that](https://www.icj-cij.org/sites/default/files/case-related/178/178-20261119-sum-01-00-en.pdf), among other atrocities, the court found that “widespread acts of extreme violence were perpetrated by the Myanmar security forces against children in northern Rakhine State,” that “in addition to the extreme hardship of the journey, the Myanmar security forces systematically shot at Rohingya as they were fleeing,” and that “the evidence demonstrates a deliberate, organized process” of destroying Rohingya villages.

“The only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the group,” Judge Iwasawa read from the ruling.

The court said that Myanmar must provide restitution — trying to put things back as they were, including through allowing return and reunification — and, where that fails, compensation. But the amount of compensation needed is not yet set, and will be determined in further proceedings.

The court does not have the power to enforce its own rulings, and the U.N. Security Council would need to uphold the decision. Two members of the Security Council, China and Russia, may opt to protect Myanmar. Each provides Myanmar with weapons it now uses to kill civilians in the civil war.

“Concerned governments” should “press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar,” Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch, said in a written statement following the announcement.

Notably, the United States [has previously said](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/03/21/us/politics/myanmar-genocide-biden.html) that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, though that happened during the Biden administration.

“I think that you’re going to see relatively powerful states putting pressure on Myanmar,” said Ms. McIntyre, of Adelaide University. “How much they pay heed to that pressure is a question.”

Thursday’s decision was greeted by some in the international legal community as a sign that justice can still be served on a global stage, even as the Trump administration attacks international bodies. The administration plans [to impose sweeping sanctions](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/us/politics/trump-international-criminal-court-sanctions.html) against another tribunal, the International Criminal Court, which could severely impair the court’s ability to function on a day-to-day basis.

“At a moment when international law and the institutions that uphold it face growing pressure, the Court’s decision reaffirms the vital role they play in establishing truth,” James Goldston, the executive director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, said in a statement.

For the Rohingya now in Bangladesh, the news was welcome. Yet tragedies continued after 2016 and 2017, the years ruled a genocide by the I.C.J.

Mohammed Yeasin said his wife and sister were killed in a drone attack in August 2024. The perpetrators were not the Myanmar military but the armed group from the Rakhine ethnic minority that shares its homeland with the Rohingya.

“I am happy about the I.C.J.,” he said. “But I don’t know when my sorrows will end.”

Jonathan Wolfe, Marlise Simons and Saikou Jammeh contributed reporting.

items.title: Anthropic Debuts on Wall Street as a $2 Trillion Company
items.summary: The San Francisco company was the first major A.I. lab to go public in a highly anticipated moment for the tech industry.
items.full_text:
Title: Anthropic Debuts on Wall Street as a $2 Trillion Company - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/technology/anthropic-2-trillion.html

Published Time: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 18:16:22 GMT

Markdown Content:
Anthropic joined the ranks of the world’s most valuable public companies Thursday, making its stock market debut with an initial market capitalization of about $2 trillion, marking a rapid ascent for a start-up founded during the pandemic by artificial intelligence researchers who strongly believed in the potential of the technology.

Wall Street investors clamored for shares in the company, which many view as a bellwether for A.I.’s future. Anthropic’s share price opened on Nasdaq at $111.50, up 34 percent from its initial public offering, which made Anthropic by far the fastest company in history to surpass a trillion-dollar market cap. It traded down to about $100 a share within its first hour on the stock market.

The company’s soaring stock price contrasts with an anxious moment for investors, as they question whether the A.I. market is in a debt-fueled bubble, whether regulation will slow down the industry, the impact of Jensen Huang’s departure at the chip supplier Nvidia, and rising public sentiment against A.I.

“We’ve been calm about it,” Dario Amodei, chief executive officer of Anthropic, said in an interview on CNBC Thursday morning. “We think we’re building something great, so the day-to-day, week-to-week, even month-to-month it’s less important than the fundamentals.”

Corporate America’s rapid embrace of Anthropic’s A.I. tools drove investors’ interest in the stock. Anthropic had no revenue at the start of 2023, before the commercial debut of its chatbot Claude, before growing to more than $33 billion in sales in the first nine months of this year.

Anthropic, founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees who left that A.I. lab before it released ChatGPT, wasn’t initially as synonymous with the A.I. boom as its older rival. But Anthropic’s focus on building technology for business customers, rather than consumers, paid off as its revenue ballooned over the past two years.

Tech investors said they had seen nothing like Anthropic’s ascent from fledgling start-up to corporate behemoth.

“Anthropic has speed-run the entire process faster than probably any other company in the history of capitalism,” said Lillian Li, an investor in the Scottish fund manager Baillie Gifford, which first invested privately in Anthropic last year and sought to invest in its I.P.O. She added: “The explosion of revenue surprised quite a lot of folks, perhaps even themselves.”

Ms. Li said she first met with Anthropic leaders in 2023, when it was barely a business. Their pitch — that its A.I. would quickly be capable of handling a variety of work tasks on its own — “seemed slightly like science fiction,” she added.

The listing will spray cash around Silicon Valley. Anthropic had raised $130 billion from roughly 300 investors as a private company, according to PitchBook, which tracks investment activity. Many of the company’s investors made their biggest bet ever as the company gobbled up cash.

One firm, Iconiq, passed on the opportunity to invest until it saw Anthropic’s adoption by customers and the progress its A.I. models were making. In late 2025, the firm decided to “lean in with everything we have,” said Matthew Jacobson, a partner at the firm. Iconiq invested $6 billion and became one of Anthropic’s largest shareholders.

The I.P.O. mints at least eight billionaires among Anthropic’s founders and executives, who were relative unknowns until the last few years.

Each of Anthropic’s seven founders — including Mr. Amodei, the former Bloomberg journalist Jack Clark and the Johns Hopkins University physics professor Jared Kaplan — is worth about $25 billion, the company’s offering prospectus indicated. They have each pledged to give away 80 percent of their personal equity in Anthropic.

Many Anthropic employees are in line for enormous paydays as well. Anthropic employees who joined between 2021 and 2023, for instance, could buy shares for about 50 cents each, on average, the prospectus said. They would be able to sell those shares for more than 160 times what they paid after the I.P.O.

Employees could begin to sell a portion of their stakes on Thursday, a shift from the customary practice of companies’ forcing workers and other existing shareholders to wait months before they can sell stock.

“I cannot think of any significant I.P.O. that has ever had an immediate release of some of the shares,” said Jay Ritter, a University of Florida professor who studies I.P.O.s. “Anthropic has the bargaining power to demand that” from the investment banks working on the deal, he added.

The I.P.O. gives Anthropic more cash to buy chips, energy and other infrastructure it needs to train new A.I. models and serve customers in its business, which is expensive to operate.

The company has already committed to spend about $900 billion on data center infrastructure over the next two decades, and Wall Street is expecting more bills to pile up. That makes Anthropic one of the most important companies driving a data-center build out that makes up a growing portion of U.S. economic growth.

Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a Columbia business school finance professor, said Anthropic’s I.P.O. is a “watershed moment for this build out.” He has forecast that companies were committing more money to A.I. infrastructure over the next several years, relative to the U.S. economy, than they did in past investment booms that built railways, highways and telecommunications infrastructure.

Stock analysts at Goldman Sachs, the investment bank running the I.P.O., told investors in recent weeks they expected Anthropic [to burn cash aggressively](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/technology/anthropic-ipo-spending-plans.html) in the coming years. They said they expected Anthropic to surpass $440 billion in annual revenue by 2029, more sales than Apple generated last year.

Anthropic executives spent the last two weeks selling investors on their vision for what’s to come, including the company’s nascent efforts to use its A.I. models to discover new pharmaceuticals and build robotic systems. It is also starting to sell its own software applications to automate portions of white-collar work, like design, finance and legal tasks.

“For me, that revenue trajectory only begins to make sense if they branch out to all kinds of new products,” Dr. Van Nieuwerburgh said. He added that competition to sell A.I. products could intensify.

“They have a huge target on their back,” he said.
